ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: The figure shows several identical regular pentagons connected along edges, forming an unfinished ring-shaped structure. The inner boundary of the ring is composed of the exposed edges of these regular pentagons facing the center; at the visible vertices of the inner boundary, it can be seen that the vertices of two regular pentagons meet, and the remaining angle belongs to the regular polygon of the middle hole. Then reason: The perimeter of each regular pentagon is 65, so each side length is 65/5=13. The interior angle of a regular pentagon is (5-2)×180/5=108°. At a vertex of the inner boundary, a full circle around it is 360°, of which there are two interior angles of regular pentagons, namely 108°+108°, therefore the interior angle of the middle regular polygon at that vertex is 360°-216°=144°. Suppose this inner-boundary regular polygon has n sides, then its interior angle is 180(n-2)/n, so 180(n-2)/n=144. Solving gives 180n-360=144n, 36n=360, n=10. Each side of the inner boundary is one side of a regular pentagon, with length 13, therefore P=10×13=130.

method.method_draft: First read the diagram as showing a partial edge-to-edge ring of identical regular pentagons: the inner boundary is made from exposed sides of the pentagons, and at each visible corner of the hole two pentagon vertices meet. From the text, each pentagon has perimeter 65, so its side length is 65/5 = 13. A regular pentagon has interior angle 108 degrees. At an inner-boundary vertex, the full 360 degrees around the point is split into two pentagon angles, 108 + 108, plus the angle of the inner regular polygon. Thus the inner angle is 360 - 216 = 144 degrees. A regular n-gon with interior angle 144 satisfies 180(n-2)/n = 144, giving n = 10. Since each side of the inner polygon is one pentagon side, P = 10 * 13 = 130.
